claims.text: The initially solid nanoparticles are homogeneous, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloys.
Controlled heating induces atomic-scale chemical rearrangements in the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Heating produces localized compositional fluctuations or chemically distinct nanodomains.
Preferential segregation and compositional fluctuations create localized regions of reduced cohesive energy.
Heating facilitates atomic diffusion within the nanoparticles.
Elements with lower melting points preferentially accumulate at the surface or in specific nanodomains.
Local reduction of cohesive energy triggers localized premelting.
Localized premelting regions act as nucleation sites from which full melting progresses.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles exhibit a two-stage or broadened melting transition.
In situ TEM should reveal early localized surface or domain melting in the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
EDS mapping should reveal significant surface or local compositional changes during heating.
DSC should reveal a distinct two-stage melting profile for the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Comparable monometallic nanoparticles are expected to melt more uniformly and without a clear premelting stage.
The proposed behavior applies primarily to nanoscale equiatomic high-entropy-alloy particles for which surface-to-volume effects and atomic mobility are significant.
The proposed behavior may not extend to bulk materials or sufficiently large particles where nanoscale surface effects are negligible.
